chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Standing becomes difficult for me during prayer. He said: 'When you wish to attain the prayer of the one standing, recite while you are sitting. When two verses of the Surah remain, then stand, complete what remains, bow, and prostrate; that is the prayer of the one standing.'

al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about a man who recited Al-Hamd and half of the Surah in the first rak'ah. Is it sufficient for him in the second rak'ah not to recite Al-Hamd and instead recite what remains of the Surah? He said: 'He must recite Al-Hamd, then recite what remains of the Surah.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This narration is applicable to voluntary prayers (nafl), because we have clarified that in obligatory prayers (fard), one does not recite less than a full Surah along with Al-Hamd.
ai.seo_question: How should one pray if standing is difficult, and is Al-Fatiha still required?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the principle of *rukūʿ* (standing) as a core pillar of prayer, allowing the recitation to be completed while seated if standing becomes burdensome, provided the final two verses are recited while standing. The juristic distinction that this flexibility primarily applies to *nawāfil* (voluntary) prayers, whereas obligatory prayers require a full Surah plus Al-Hamd, reflects the Shafi'i and Shia consensus on the minimum recitation requirements. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on ease (*taysīr*) without compromising the structural integrity of the prayer.
